claims.text: Evidence does not support implementing digital screen limits of less than 1 or 2 hours per day recommended by the AAP after controlling for demographic and socioeconomic covariates.
Digital screen time is linked to caregiver attachment via small parabolic functions.
Digital screen time is linked to positive affect via small parabolic functions.

evidence.description: Evidence did not support implementing limits (< 1 or < 2 hr/day) as recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics, once variability in child ethnicity, age, gender, household income, and caregiver educational attainment were considered.
Small parabolic functions linked screen time to attachment.
Small parabolic functions linked screen time to positive affect.

methodologies.name: Population-Based Parent Telephone Interviews
methodologies.description: Cross-sectional assessment of young children's screen engagement and psychological well-being reported by parents via telephone interviews.
datasets: 19,957 telephone interviews with parents of 2- to 5-year-olds
conditions: Controlling for variability in child ethnicity, age, gender, household income, and caregiver educational attainment

limitations.text: There is little empirical understanding of how young children's screen engagement links to their well-being.

future_work.text: Conduct a critical cost-benefit analysis to determine whether setting firm screen time limits constitutes a judicious use of caregiver and professional resources.
